newsitem.title: PERU: Peru mining sales go ahead despite hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru mining sales go ahead despite hostage crisis.

text.p: Crisis? What crisis?

Gun-toting Marxist rebels holding 72 VIP captives for six weeks at the Japanese ambassador's home have hardly raised an eyebrow among privatization officials, who insist it's business as usual conducting Peru's program of mining asset sell-offs.

Despite early fears the hostage crisis would scare away potential buyers, the government has put its faith in investor confidence and continued announcing new sales' dates for this years' sweeping privatization program.
"The privatization of (state miner) Minero Peru goes ahead," said company chief Jorge Kawamura in an interview. "We cannot put off a process whose very aim is the country's development."

Therefore, as the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) lambasts Peru's free market reforms from inside the besieged diplomatic home, Kawamura sends bidding details to firms interested in February's Bayovar phosphate deposit sale.

Unperturbed by the rebels, 25 miners -- including various from the United States, Canada and Mexico -- have pre-qualified to bid for the estimated 262 million tonnes of phosphate reserves, according to the government.

Since December 17, when 15 heavily armed rebels stormed a reception at the Japanese residence, President Alberto Fujimori has repeatedly claimed the hostage crisis was an "isolated" incident that would not affect investment in Peru.
Enrique Olivares, spokesman for the government's second miner, Centromin, agreed.
"Our (sales) program continues," Olivares said. "We are putting the final details on the schedule for the year. The confidence shown by investors in the country encourages us."

That confidence should bring the government $5.75 billion -- from direct cash payments and buyers' investment commitments -- through its mining sales in the next three years, according to the privatization board, COPRI.

Underlining its optimism in investor confidence, Centromin said Monday it was pressing ahead with the sale of its largest asset. The state miner announced it will auction its huge, outdated La Oroya metallurgic complex April 14.

Under the provisional auction terms, the new owner of La Oroya would pay a small purchase fee to become the majority owner in a mixed company with the government and would then gradually receive more shares as the buyer injects fresh capital, officials said.
The La Oroya complex of smelters and refineries, based in the central Andes at 12,100 feet (3,700 meters) processes 22 different metals and byproducts.
Following the La Oroya sale, Centromin hopes to set a date for the auction of a 100 percent stake in its San Cristobal and Andaychagua mines as one asset.
By mid-1997, the government also plans to sell Centromin's remaining four mines, a railroad network, port facilities, four hydroelectric plants and several prospects.
There is every indication Centromin will find buyers for its list of attractive properties.

The 1994 attempt to sell Centromin as a whole failed to interest a single bidder. But last year, Centromin's relaunched, piecemeal privatization yielded rewards far exceeding expectations. The auctions attracted the world's largest mining companies to pay hundreds of millions of dollars and make investment commitments worth billions.

Minero Peru hopes to match its sister company's success with its own swathe of sales this year. Centromin's sell-off program includes operating assets as well as deposits, while Kawamura's company only sells deposits.

After launching its own piecemeal sell-off program in 1992, Minero Peru has already offloaded the lion's share of its assets. But this year, the miner plans to sell its most remaining important units.
Following the sale of Bayovar, Kawamura said he is confident investors will buy both the gold-copper Michiquillay deposit and the Winicocha gold deposit by mid-year.

Then the state miner plans to auction its Alto Chicama coal reserve in the second half of the year and finally its Las Bambas copper deposit sale, which has attracted six interested firms, will be put up for auction as soon as the courts decide a dispute over the current ownership of the asset.
((-- Lima newsroom, 511 221-2134))
